subject: Dynamically Generate Plots in Conditional Tabs using renderUI

messages.author: 5e5fd7ded8be1f40
messages.subject: Dynamically Generate Plots in Conditional Tabs using renderUI
parts:
Hi All,

I need some help creating dynamic plots that go inside dynamic tabs.  Here's the situation ... I have a data file that contains digital marketing data.  The file has the following pieces of information:  Campaign Name, Channel Name, Page Views, and Visits.  Campaign Names are unique and roll up to one of four different marketing channels.  This will change in the future depending on the data I feed it (for example, I may have six marketing channels in the next file I use), but this will do for troubleshooting purposes.  I want to dynamically create tabs and output for each marketing channel in the file.  I have been able to figure out how to create the tabs, but I'm having a hard time figuring out how to create other types of output (like a plot) to go with each tab.

The tabs were created using renderUI in the following code in the server file:

 output$mytabs = renderUI({
    if(is.null(rawData())){return ()}
    channels = unique(rawData()$Channel)
    myTabs = lapply(channels, tabPanel)
    do.call(tabsetPanel, myTabs)
  })

These were then referenced in the ui file as follows:

   tabPanel("Parameters & Model Fit",
               uiOutput('mytabs')

Ultimately, I'd like to plot Page Views vs Visits for each Marketing Channel.  In my global file, I've created two functions -- one function plots one channel at a time and another function that plots all the channels and saves each one as separate elements within a list.  I'm not sure which one of these will end up being useful.  You'll notice the "Testing" tab in the ui that just shows that my plots actually do generate.

I have tried a number of different things to try and get plots to show up in each tab, but to no avail.  I've attached my code including a snippet to create a csv file that you can use with the upload data function.  Any help would be greatly appreciated!!!

Thanks!
Jess

Thanks,

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: Dynamically Generate Plots in Conditional Tabs using renderUI
parts:
Hi Jessica,

I only looked at the second pair of ui/server files. I have a number of suggestions that will hopefully clear up some things.
  1. Why do you have a runApp.R? And why does your server.R source global.R? The contents of ui.R, server.R, and global.R are correct, but you should just do shiny::runApp() to run the app--no need to have your own script to do what Shiny already wants to do for you.
  2. In server.R, you do a lot of `if (is.null(whatever)) return()`. Instead you should use req in your rawData reactive;, which will let you remove all of those checks.
  3. In your output$mytabs, your lapply is just creating a list of empty tabs. Instead, it should be creating a list of tabs that each contain a plotOutput("plot", i), something like:
    myTabs <- lapply(channels, function(ch) {
      tabPanel(ch,
        plotOutput(paste0("plot", i))
      )
    })
    (you'd need to increment i--hopefully you get the idea).
  4. The createPlots is almost right, but, it shouldn't be a reactive that's called from scatterPlot; it should be an observer instead. I strongly encourage you to watch the Effective Reactive Programming 1 & 2 tutorials here.
  5. Also in createPlots, the logic here is fine except that you can get away from the for/local/my_i pattern by using lapply(seq_along(channels), function(i) { ... }) instead.

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: Dynamically Generate Plots in Conditional Tabs using renderUI
parts:
OK, a couple of things.

do.call takes a function (any function), and a list of objects, and calls the function as if those objects were the arguments. For example,

do.call(read.csv, list("data.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE))

is equivalent to

read.csv("data.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

It's convenient to do this when we're dynamically assembling the arguments to the function, as we're doing now.

lapply(channels, tabPanel) is equivalent to calling:

list(
  tabPanel(channel[1]),
  tabPanel(channel[2]),
  tabPanel(channel[3]),
  # and so on...
)

So those two lines together amount to:

tabsetPanel(
  tabPanel(channel[1]),
  tabPanel(channel[2]),
  tabPanel(channel[3]),
  # and so on...
)

Those tabPanels are empty though, which isn't useful. What you want is a whole bunch of stuff in each tabPanel, right? So instead of calling lapply(channels, tabPanel), you want that second argument not to be tabPanel but a function that generates a tabPanel that contains plotOutputs and whatever else you want to put into each tab.

That function will need not only the channel name, but also what position they're at in the list, since you're going to name the plot outputs plot_1, plot_2, etc. One way to do that is to use an mapply instead of lapply:

myTabs <- mapply(1:length(channels), channels, FUN = function(i, channel) {
  tabPanel(channel,
    plotOutput(paste0("plot_", i)),
    tableOutput(paste0("table_", i))
  )
})

So after the do.call you'll end up with something like

tabsetPanel(
  tabPanel(channel[1],
    plotOutput("plot_1"),
    tableOutput("table_1")
  ),
  tabPanel(channel[2],
    plotOutput("plot_2"),
    tableOutput("table_2")
  )
)

which is hopefully close to what you want.

lapply(channels, tabPanel) is equivalent to calling:

list(
  tabPanel(channel[1]),
  tabPanel(channel[2]),
  tabPanel(channel[3]),
  # and so on...
)

So those two lines together amount to:

tabsetPanel(
  tabPanel(channel[1]),
  tabPanel(channel[2]),
  tabPanel(channel[3]),
  # and so on...
)

Those tabPanels are empty though, which isn't useful. What you want is a whole bunch of stuff in each tabPanel, right? So instead of calling lapply(channels, tabPanel), you want that second argument not to be tabPanel but a function that generates a tabPanel that contains plotOutputs and whatever else you want to put into each tab.

That function will need not only the channel name, but also what position they're at in the list, since you're going to name the plot outputs plot_1, plot_2, etc. One way to do that is to use an mapply instead of lapply:

myTabs <- mapply(1:length(channels), channels, FUN = function(i, channel) {
  tabPanel(channel,
    plotOutput(paste0("plot_", i)),
    tableOutput(paste0("table_", i))
  )
})

So after the do.call you'll end up with something like

tabsetPanel(
  tabPanel(channel[1],
    plotOutput("plot_1"),
    tableOutput("table_1")
  ),
  tabPanel(channel[2],
    plotOutput("plot_2"),
    tableOutput("table_2")
  )
)

which is hopefully close to what you want.

I only looked at the second pair of ui/server files. I have a number of suggestions that will hopefully clear up some things.
  1. Why do you have a runApp.R? And why does your server.R source global.R? The contents of ui.R, server.R, and global.R are correct, but you should just do shiny::runApp() to run the app--no need to have your own script to do what Shiny already wants to do for you.
  2. In server.R, you do a lot of `if (is.null(whatever)) return()`. Instead you should use req in your rawData reactive;, which will let you remove all of those checks.
  3. In your output$mytabs, your lapply is just creating a list of empty tabs. Instead, it should be creating a list of tabs that each contain a plotOutput("plot", i), something like:
    myTabs <- lapply(channels, function(ch) {
      tabPanel(ch,
        plotOutput(paste0("plot", i))
      )
    })
    (you'd need to increment i--hopefully you get the idea).
  4. The createPlots is almost right, but, it shouldn't be a reactive that's called from scatterPlot; it should be an observer instead. I strongly encourage you to watch the Effective Reactive Programming 1 & 2 tutorials here.
  5. Also in createPlots, the logic here is fine except that you can get away from the for/local/my_i pattern by using lapply(seq_along(channels), function(i) { ... }) instead.
